{{Short description|Integer sequence in number theory}}
In [[number theory]]<!--mathematics-->, a '''Descartes number''' is an [[odd number]] which would have been an [[odd perfect number]] if one of its [[composite number|composite]] [[divisor|factors]] were [[prime number|prime]]. They are named after [[René Descartes]], who observed that the number  {{math|''D'' {{=}} 3<sup>2</sup> ⋅ 7<sup>2</sup> ⋅ 11<sup>2</sup> ⋅ 13<sup>2</sup> ⋅ 22021 {{=}} (3⋅1001)<sup>2</sup>&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;(22⋅1001 − 1) {{=}} 198585576189}} would be an odd perfect number if only {{math|22021}} were a [[prime number]], since in that case the [[sum-of-divisors function]] for {{math| ''D'' }} would satisfy
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\sigma(D) 
&= (3^2+3+1)\cdot(7^2+7+1)\cdot(11^2+11+1)\cdot(13^2+13+1)\cdot(22021+1) \\
&= (13)\cdot(3\cdot19)\cdot(7\cdot19)\cdot(3\cdot61)\cdot(22\cdot1001) \\
&= 3^2\cdot7\cdot13\cdot19^2\cdot61\cdot(22\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13) \\ &= 2 \cdot (3^2\cdot7^2\cdot11^2\cdot13^2) \cdot (19^2\cdot61)  \\ &= 2 \cdot (3^2\cdot7^2\cdot11^2\cdot13^2) \cdot 22021 = 2D.
\end{align}</math>
In reality, 22021 is composite ({{math|22021 {{=}} 19<sup>2</sup>&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;61}}), and <math>\sigma(D) = 426027470778 = \frac{23622}{11011} D</math>.

A Descartes number is defined as an odd number {{math|''n'' {{=}} ''m''&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;''p''}} where {{math| ''m'' }} and {{math| ''p'' }} are [[coprime]] and {{math|2''n'' {{=}} ''σ''(''m'')&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;(''p'' + 1)}}, whence {{math|''p''}} is taken as a 'spoof' prime. The example given is the only one currently known.

If {{math|''m''}} is an odd [[almost perfect number]],<ref>Currently, the only known almost perfect numbers are the non-negative [[powers of 2]], whence the only known odd almost perfect number is {{math|2<sup>0</sup> {{=}} 1.}}</ref> that is, {{math|σ(''m'') {{=}} 2''m'' − 1}} and {{math| 2''m'' − 1 }} is taken as a 'spoof' prime, then {{math|''n'' {{=}} ''m''&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;(2''m'' − 1)}} is a Descartes number, since {{math|σ(''n'') {{=}} σ(''m''&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;(2''m'' − 1)) {{=}} σ(''m'')&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;2''m'' {{=}} (2''m'' − 1)&thinsp;⋅&thinsp;2''m'' {{=}} 2''n''}}. If {{math|2''m'' − 1}} were prime, {{math|''n''}} would be an odd perfect number.

==Properties==
If {{math|''n''}} is a [[cube-free]] Descartes number not [[divisible]] by {{math|3}}, then {{math|''n''}} has over one million distinct prime divisors.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Banks |first1=William D. |chapter=Descartes numbers |date=2008 |title=Anatomy of integers. Based on the CRM workshop, Montreal, Canada, March 13–17, 2006 |pages=167–173 |place=Providence, RI |publisher=American Mathematical Society (AMS) |language=English |isbn=978-0-8218-4406-9 |last2=Güloğlu |first2=Ahmet M. |last3=Nevans |first3=C. Wesley |last4=Saidak |first4=Filip|zbl=1186.11004 }}</ref>  If <math>D=pq</math> is a Descartes number other than Descartes' example, with spoof-prime factor <math>p</math>, then <math>q > 10^{12}</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Tóth|2021}}</ref>

==Generalizations==

[[John Voight (mathematician)|John Voight]] generalized Descartes numbers to allow negative bases. He found the example <math>3^4 7^2 11^2 19^2 (-127)^1 </math>.<ref name="Quanta">{{cite news |last1=Nadis |first1=Steve |title=Mathematicians Open a New Front on an Ancient Number Problem |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-open-a-new-front-on-an-ancient-number-problem-20200910/ |access-date=3 October 2021 |work=Quanta Magazine |date=September 10, 2020}}</ref>  Subsequent work by a group at [[Brigham Young University]] found more examples similar to Voight's example,<ref name="Quanta"/> and also allowed a new class of spoofs where one is allowed to also not notice that a prime is the same as another prime in the factorization.<ref name="BYU">{{cite journal |author1=Andersen, Nickolas|author2= Durham, Spencer|author3= Griffin, Michael J.|author4= Hales, Jonathan|author5= Jenkins, Paul|author6= Keck, Ryan|author7= Ko, Hankun|author8= Molnar, Grant|author9= Moss, Eric|author10= Nielsen, Pace P.|author11= Niendorf, Kyle|author12= Tombs, Vandy|author13= Warnick, Merrill|author14= Wu, Dongsheng |title=Odd, spoof perfect factorizations |journal=J. Number Theory |year=2020 |issue=234 |pages=31–47|arxiv=2006.10697 }}</ref> A generalization of Descartes numbers to [[multiply perfect number|multiperfect numbers]] has also been constructed. ({{harvtxt|Tóth|2025}}).
